# House runtime

A small JavaScript fantasy console: 256×192 (shown 4× on the Picade 10"'s 1024×768 panel, D81), 32 fixed colors, 4-voice chip synth, the cabinet's buttons, deterministic under test. Design: D3, D10, D11, D13, D21 and D50 in [../docs/decisions.md](../docs/decisions.md).

- **Cart API:** [cart.d.ts](cart.d.ts) (`Arcade.Cart`, `Arcade.G`, `Arcade.Lib.*`)
- **Test hook:** [test-hook.d.ts](test-hook.d.ts) (`Arcade.Checks`, `Arcade.TestHandle`)
- **Starter library:** [lib/REFERENCE.md](lib/REFERENCE.md) (carts use it as `g.lib`)
- **Example:** [examples/hello/](examples/hello/) (`game.js` + `checks.js`)

## Writing a cart

A cart's `game.js` is one ES module that **imports nothing**. Its default export has four functions. All game state lives in the object `init` returns, which comes back as `s`:

```js
// @ts-check
/** @typedef {{ x: number, score: number, board: Arcade.Lib.Grid }} State */
/** @type {Arcade.Cart<State>} */
export default {
  init(g) { return { x: g.W / 2, score: 0, board: g.lib.grid.make(10, 20) }; },
  update(g, s) { if (g.btn("right")) s.x += 2; if (g.btnp("a")) g.sfx("coin"); },
  draw(g, s) { g.cls(g.colors.night); g.text(`SCORE ${s.score}`, 4, 4, g.colors.white); },
  probe(g, s) { return { x: s.x, score: s.score }; },  // what checks.js can see
};
```

- **The clock** is a fixed 60 Hz. `update` runs once per frame, then `draw`. `g.frame` counts frames.
- **Input:**
  - `g.btn(b, p)` is true while a button is held;
  - `g.btnp(b, p)` is true on the frame it's pressed;
  - `g.btnr(b, p)` is true on the frame it's released.
  
  Buttons are `up down left right a b x y start`, and `p` is the player, 1 to 8 (default 1).
- **Players (D110–D113):** `g.players` is how many controllers the console has: **1 on the cabinet**, and 1 by default everywhere else. Games are single player by default. A player with no controller holds nothing (`g.btn("a", 2)` is false at `g.players === 1`), so a game for two people takes turns with `g.lib.turns`, which hands over controller 1 between turns.
- **Drawing** on 256×192 (`g.W`, `g.H`; use those, never the numbers), with colors 0–31 or by name (`g.colors.red`):
  - shapes: `cls pset pget line rect rectfill circ circfill`;
  - text: `text(s, x, y, c, {scale, align})` and `textWidth`;
  - sprites: `sprite(rows)` and `spr(s, x, y, {flipX, flipY, scale, color})`. In sprite rows, `0`–`9` and `a`–`v` are colors 0–31 and `.` is transparent;
  - view: `camera`, `clip`.
- **Randomness:** `g.rand()`, `g.rnd(n)` and `g.pick(arr)`. These are seeded, so tests reproduce. Never use `Math.random`.
- **Sound:** `g.sfx(name)` takes `blip select jump coin pop hit explode powerup lose win`. Also `g.tone({ note: "C5", wave, frames, vol, slide })` and `g.stop()`.
- **Colors outside 0–31** still draw (wrapped), but each one is reported once as a dev warning (`t.warnings()`, `arcade.warnings`, the browser console), so the playtest's palette check can flag it.
- **Saves:** `g.save(data)` and `g.load()` hold one JSON value of at most 4 KB, e.g. for a high score.
- **Library:** `g.lib.grid`, `g.lib.collide`, `g.lib.timers`, `g.lib.score`, `g.lib.flow` and `g.lib.turns`. See [lib/REFERENCE.md](lib/REFERENCE.md). Types are `Arcade.Lib.Grid`, `Arcade.Lib.Piece`, `Arcade.Lib.Timer` and so on.
- **Not allowed:** `document`, `window`, `fetch`, timers, `eval` and imports. The frame's sandbox blocks them anyway, and the type-check flags them.

`checks.js` has one async check per `(auto)` rule id. A check fails by throwing, and the message becomes the reason in the report. See [test-hook.d.ts](test-hook.d.ts) and [examples/hello/checks.js](examples/hello/checks.js).

Commands (package.json `bin`):

- `arcade-run <game.js> [--frames N] [--seed N] [--players N] [--input JSON] [--checks checks.js]` runs the cart headless and prints `{ ok, frame, hash, probe, sounds, warnings, checks }`. It exits 1 on a cart error or a failed check.
- `arcade-dev-server [--port N] [--cart name=dir]` serves carts for a browser (below).
- Type-check a cart with no DOM: `tsc -p runtime/tsconfig.cart.json`, or copy that config for your cart folder.

## Play a cart

```sh
export PATH=/opt/homebrew/opt/node@22/bin:$PATH
node runtime/dev-server.js                       # serves runtime/examples/* on :8320
node runtime/dev-server.js --cart mine=~/game-studio-data/carts/mine --port 8320
open "http://127.0.0.1:8320/runtime/play.html?cart=/carts/hello/game.js&fps=1"
```

Keyboard (dev):

| Player | Stick | A | B | X | Y | START |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | arrows | Z | X | C | V | Enter |
| P2 | W A S D | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

Only players up to `?players=N` (default 1) get input, so add `&players=2` to use the P2 keys. Escape is ★, the leave-game key (the Picade's ESC button, D88): it goes to the host as `onStar` and never reaches the cart. Gamepads use the standard mapping: pad *k* is player *k*+1 (pad 0 is P1), for pads below `players`; guide on any pad is ★. The face buttons are A B X Y (0 1 2 3), START is 9, and the stick is the d-pad or the left stick (dead zone 0.5). Guide is ★.

`play.html` parameters:

- `cart`: the URL path of `game.js` on the same server (the frame's CSP is `script-src 'self'`).
- `seed`: default 1.
- `players`: how many controllers, 1–8 (default 1, like the cabinet). The cabinet passes its config's `players` to `createHost({ players })`.
- `test=1`: a paused clock and no live input. Frames only advance through `arcade.test.step()`.
- `save=<url-encoded JSON>`: the initial `g.load()` value.
- `fps=1`: show the fps, the scale and the tick count.

## Driving it from code

**Headless (Node, no browser).** This is the fastest way to run checks:

```js
import { headless } from "@game-studio-arcade/runtime";
const t = await headless("path/to/game.js", { seed: 1 }); // { players: 2 } for two controllers
await t.input([{ frames: 30, p1: "right" }]);
await t.step(30);
console.log(await t.probe(), (await t.frame()).hash);
```

**Browser (Playwright).** The contract the playtest relies on, kept stable:

```js
import { startServer } from "@game-studio-arcade/runtime/dev-server";
const s = await startServer({ port: 0, carts: { mine: "/abs/path/to/cart" } });
await page.goto(`${s.url}/runtime/play.html?cart=/carts/mine/game.js&seed=1&test=1`);
await page.waitForFunction(() => window.arcade);
await page.evaluate(() => window.arcade.ready);            // rejects with the load/init error
await page.evaluate(() => window.arcade.test.step(60));
const frame = await page.evaluate(() => window.arcade.test.frame()); // pixels: plain number[]
await s.close();
```

- `startServer({ port = 8320, host = "127.0.0.1", carts = {}, root })` resolves to `{ url, port, close() }`. Port 0 picks a free port.
- `createHandler(sameOptions)` returns a `(req, res)` handler to mount in another server.
- Routes: `/runtime/…` is this folder, `/carts/<name>/…` is each cart folder, and `/…` is `root` if given.
- Every response has `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (the sandboxed frame has an opaque origin) and `Cache-Control: no-store`.
- `window.arcade` is set synchronously.
- `arcade.state` is `"loading" | "ready" | "error"`.
- `arcade.errors` collects every uncaught cart error as `{ message, stack, where, frame }`.
- `arcade.test` is the same `t` as headless. For a fresh cart, call `t.reset()` or reload the page.

## How it fits together

```
host page (play.html + src/host.js)            sandboxed iframe (frame.html + src/frame.js)
  owns: 60 Hz clock, keyboard/gamepad,  ─tick{n, masks}─▶  machine: update ×n, draw, render canvas
        WebAudio synth, saves           ◀─out{audio, save}─
  window.arcade.test  ─call{method,args}─▶  test handle (src/testhandle.js) ─result─▶
```

- **`src/machine.js`** is the console core: the `g` object, framebuffer, RNG, input edges, voices and the save slot. It has no DOM and no timers. Headless Node and the frame both run it, which is why their frame hashes match.
- **The host** accumulates fixed 60 Hz ticks on `requestAnimationFrame`, allowing 4 ms of slack so a 16.5 ms frame still gets exactly one tick. A key tapped and released between two ticks still counts as held for one frame.
- **Sandbox:** `sandbox="allow-scripts"` with no same-origin, plus CSP `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'`. A cart can't fetch, use storage, cookies or eval, load images or remote modules, or reach the host page.

## Tests

`npm test` (from the repo root or `runtime/`) covers:

- input mapping (keyboard, gamepad, scripts);
- the palette;
- determinism (same seed and input give the same hashes; a different seed or input gives different ones);
- the `g` API, saves and errors;
- the dev server;
- the starter library.

`tsconfig.cart.json` type-checks carts the way `validate_cart` should, with no DOM and no Node types.
# studio-kit/spec

The cart spec format (D1, D11, D30), the tools that read it, and `validate_cart` (D31).

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [template.md](template.md) | The `spec.md` every cart starts from. |
| [writing-rules.md](writing-rules.md) | How to write `(auto)` and `(you check)` rules, with good and bad examples. |
| [checks-format.md](checks-format.md) | The `checks.js` format and what `validate_cart` enforces. |
| `index.js` / `index.d.ts` | The parser, rule coverage and validateCart API. |
| `bin/gsa-spec.js` | A small CLI over the parser and rule coverage. |
| `bin/validate-cart.js` | `validate_cart`: cart.json, rule coverage, the D13 lint and the cart type check. |

## API

```js
import { parseSpec, formatSpec, rulesOf, validateRuleCoverage, validateCart } from '@game-studio-arcade/spec';

const spec = parseSpec(text);       // { title, byline, sections, rules, assumptions, changelog, errors, warnings }; never throws
formatSpec(spec);                   // canonical text; formatSpec(parseSpec(t)) === t for canonical t
rulesOf(text);                      // [{ id: 'R1', kind: 'auto' | 'you-check', text }]
await validateRuleCoverage(cartDir); // { ok, rules, checks, errors, warnings }: the rule-coverage part of validate_cart
await validateCart(cartDir);        // { ok, cart, rules, checks, errors, warnings }: all of validate_cart (D31)
```

`validateCart(dir, { types: false })` skips the tsc pass; by default a missing tsc is an error. Every issue has `file`, `line`, `check` (`coverage`, `cart.json`, `lint`, `types`) and `message`; `formatIssues(report)` gives one line each. The parts are exported too: `checkCartJson(text)`, `lintCartSource(src, {file})`, `typeCheckCart(dir, {files})`.

`checkCoverage(rules, checkIds)` is the pure comparison; `readCheckIds(path)` reads a `checks.js`'s keys in a restricted child process (see D30).

## CLI

```sh
node studio-kit/spec/bin/gsa-spec.js check  path/to/spec.md    # errors and warnings
node studio-kit/spec/bin/gsa-spec.js rules  path/to/spec.md    # rules as JSON
node studio-kit/spec/bin/gsa-spec.js format path/to/spec.md    # canonical form
node studio-kit/spec/bin/gsa-spec.js coverage path/to/cart/    # coverage report as JSON; exit 1 on errors

node studio-kit/spec/bin/validate-cart.js path/to/cart/         # one line per problem; exit 0 valid, 1 not, 2 usage
node studio-kit/spec/bin/validate-cart.js path/to/cart/ --json  # the full report
```

The type check needs `tsc`: the repo's `typescript` devDependency, or a global `tsc` on PATH (the sandbox has one, D18). Nothing is installed.

## Tests

`npm test` here (or at the root) type-checks and runs `node:test` over the template and the fixtures in `test/fixtures/` (`valid-cart/` is the cart that passes all of validate_cart; the tests break copies of it). No dependencies, so the package runs as-is in the offline sandbox.
# studio-kit/playtest

The playtest harness (D60–D63). It runs a cart's `checks.js` (one check per `(auto)` rule, D11), adds our own generic checks, saves key frames as PNG, and writes `playtest.json`.

## Run it

```sh
node studio-kit/playtest/bin/gsa-playtest.js path/to/cart            # node driver, writes path/to/cart/playtest.json
node studio-kit/playtest/bin/gsa-playtest.js path/to/cart --driver browser
node studio-kit/playtest/bin/gsa-playtest.js path/to/cart --rules R1,R3 --out /tmp/pt --json
```

**In the sandbox,** run the node driver first, then the browser driver with Playwright's global path on `NODE_PATH` (D18):

```sh
NODE_PATH="$(npm root -g)" node /workspace/kit/studio-kit/playtest/bin/gsa-playtest.js /workspace/cart --driver browser
```

Never `npm install` Playwright there; the preinstalled one is the right version.

The exit code is 0 when everything passes, 1 when a rule or generic check fails, and 2 when the harness couldn't run (no `spec.md`, no runtime, no Playwright).

Options: `--no-frames`, `--budget-ms N` (p95 frame-time budget; default 4 ms for node and 16.7 for browser, D64), `--soak-frames N` (default 600), `--seed N` (default 1), and `--runtime dir` (a runtime folder other than `../../runtime`, for development).

```js
import { playtest, comparable } from "./studio-kit/playtest/index.js";
const report = await playtest(cartDir, { driver: "node", out: null }); // out: null writes nothing
```

## What it checks

- **Rules:** each auto rule's check runs on a fresh cart (seed 1) in its own worker thread. It passes by returning and fails by throwing; the message is the reason. If the game itself throws, the reason says "the game crashed …" instead. Limits per check: 10 s of wall time (30 s in the browser) and 18,000 stepped frames.
- **Generic checks (ours, D61):** `loads`, `no-errors`, `soak` (600 frames of seeded random input on both players, plus 600 with no input), `palette` (pixels and the runtime's color warnings), `frame-time` (p95 update+draw per frame) and `deterministic` (the same seed and input must draw the same screens).

## Drivers

- `node` uses the runtime's `headless()`. It's fast and needs no browser.
- `browser` uses Playwright against `runtime/play.html?…&test=1` through `window.arcade.test`, served by `runtime/dev-server.js`. It gives the same report as `node` (the tests check this). The harness never installs Playwright (D63): it uses the copy it finds (`GSA_PLAYWRIGHT`, local `node_modules`, the global npm root, `/opt/npm-tools/node_modules`). For development, `npm install` gets 1.56.0, the sandbox's version, and `node node_modules/playwright/cli.js install --only-shell chromium` gets its browser.

## The report

`playtest.json` (D62) has `ok`, `rules` (`id`, `kind`, `text`, `status`, `passed`, `reason`, `frames`), `coverage` (spec/checks drift), `generic` (`id`, `name`, `status`, `passed`, `reason`), `frameTime`, `errors`, `warnings` (runtime dev warnings), `frames` (the PNGs in `playtest-frames/`) and `env`. `comparable(report)` drops `env` and the timing numbers. What's left must match on every machine.

## Tests

`npm test` here (or at the root). The fixtures are `dot-catch` (passes), `dot-catch-broken` (fails R1, R2, R5, `no-errors`, `soak`, `palette` and `deterministic` with readable reasons) and `hangs` (R2 loops forever). Most tests use a small stand-in runtime in `test/fake-runtime/`. The real-runtime and browser-parity tests run when `runtime/` and Playwright's Chromium are present, and are skipped otherwise.
# Context pack

What you need to build a cart on the house runtime. Read it all before you design.

1. **Cart API:** `runtime/README.md` and `runtime/cart.d.ts`.
2. **Starter library:** `runtime/lib/REFERENCE.md`, used as `g.lib`. Reuse it; don't rewrite it.
3. **Recipes:** [RECIPES.md](RECIPES.md), each from a spec rule to code, probe and check.
4. **Example carts**, complete and passing. Copy their shape, not their games:
   - [carts/dodge/](carts/dodge/) Comet Dodge: free movement, a spawner, `collide.resolve`, lives, a safe timer, a speed curve.
   - [carts/paddle/](carts/paddle/) Wall Ball: ball bounces, `collide.overlap`, a serve delay, a saved best.
   - [carts/collect/](carts/collect/) Gem Garden: a tile grid, `grid.stickStep` with `timers.repeat`, a timed round.

## A cart folder

`spec.md` (format: `studio-kit/spec/template.md`, `writing-rules.md`), `game.js` (one module, imports nothing, exports `{ init, update, draw, probe }`), `checks.js` (one async check per `(auto)` rule; `studio-kit/spec/checks-format.md`), `cart.json` (you write `{ "id": "comet-dodge", "title": "Comet Dodge", "players": 1 }`; the CLI adds the rest), and optional `assets/`.

## House conventions

- **No screen-size numbers.** Lay out from `g.W` and `g.H`, and return `W` and `H` from `probe()` for checks. A text line holds `g.W / 6` characters.
- **One player by default.** Player 1's stick, A B X Y and START; ★ never reaches the cart. A game for 2 or more people takes turns with `g.lib.turns` (REFERENCE.md). A check that needs two controllers at once calls `await t.reset({ players: 2 })` first.
- **Screens with `g.lib.flow`:** title → play → over → title. START is ignored for a screen's first 30 frames, so checks step 31 frames before pressing it.
- **Randomness from `g` only** (`g.rnd`, `g.pick`, `g.rand`). The `deterministic` check fails `Math.random` and the clock.
- **Probe what the rules talk about** (mode, positions, score, lives, timers). Checks read state, not pixels, and keep their helpers inside `checks.js`.

## Commands

From the kit root, for a cart folder `cart/`: `node studio-kit/spec/bin/validate-cart.js cart/`, then `node studio-kit/playtest/bin/gsa-playtest.js cart/`.

# Starter library reference

The house starter library gives a cart tested building blocks for collision, grids and rotation, timers, score and lives, the title → play → game-over flow, and taking turns. A cart never imports it. It's on the console handle as `g.lib` (D50):

```js
const { grid, timers, score, flow, collide, turns } = g.lib;
```

Conventions that hold everywhere:
- **State is plain data you keep.** Every helper that remembers something (a grid, a piece, a timer, a score, a flow, turns) gives you a plain JSON object to keep in your cart's state `s`. The library itself holds nothing between calls. So `probe()` can return these objects as they are, and `reset()` always starts clean.
- **Time is frames.** The clock is 60 frames per second. Tick timers once per `update`. Never use wall time.
- **`g` comes first** when a helper needs input, the frame count or saves. Everything else is pure.
- **Mutating helpers say so.** `tryMove`, `tryRotate`, `place`, `clearRows`, `resolve`, `tick` and the score functions change the object you pass them. The others return new values.

## collide: overlap, plus who destroys whom

A *box* is any object with `x, y, w, h` (top-left corner and size, in pixels). A *thing* is a box with a `kind` string, such as `"bullet"`, `"enemy"` or `"cat"`.

```js
const hitList = collide.resolve(s.things, [
  { a: "bullet", b: "enemy", kill: "both" },
  { a: "enemy", b: "player", kill: "b" },
]);
for (const h of hitList) if (h.b.kind === "enemy") score.addPoints(s.score, 10);
s.things = collide.alive(s.things);
```

### `collide.overlap(a, b)`
Returns true if boxes `a` and `b` overlap. Boxes that only touch along an edge don't count, so two 8-pixel tiles side by side at x=0 and x=8 don't collide. This is the basic test for "did these two things touch". Use it for one-off checks; use `hits` or `resolve` for whole lists.

### `collide.contains(box, px, py)`
Returns true if the point (px, py) is inside the box. The top and left edges count as inside; the bottom and right edges don't, the same as pixels. Use it for a pointer, a bullet treated as a single pixel, or a "standing on this tile?" test.

### `collide.hits(as, bs)`
Returns every overlapping pair `[a, b]` with `a` from list `as` and `b` from list `bs`, in list order. It skips anything with `dead: true`, and never pairs a thing with itself. `hits(list, list)` is therefore safe, though each pair then appears twice, once each way. Use it when you want to decide what happens yourself. `resolve` is the rule-driven version.

### `collide.resolve(things, rules)`
Applies "who destroys whom" rules to one mixed list of things. Each rule `{ a, b, kill }` names two kinds, and `kill` is `"a"`, `"b"`, `"both"` or `"none"` (`"none"` only reports the hit). Rules run in order. For each rule, every live `a`-kind thing that overlaps a live `b`-kind thing is a hit, and the matching things get `dead = true`. Anything killed earlier in the same call takes no further part, so a bullet with `kill: "both"` stops at the first enemy it hits. With `kill: "b"` a laser passes through every enemy it touches. Returns the hits as `{ a, b, rule }`, in order, for score, sound and sparkles. Call it once per update, then drop the dead with `alive`. Spec rules like "a bullet that touches an enemy destroys both" map one-to-one onto rule entries.

### `collide.alive(things)`
Returns a new array of the things whose `dead` isn't true. Call it after `resolve` (or after you set `dead` yourself) so dead things stop being drawn and updated.

## grid: boards, pieces, rotation, full rows

A *grid* is `{ w, h, cells }`, where cell (x, y) is `cells[y * w + x]`. A cell is 0 when empty; otherwise it holds any number you choose, such as a palette color or a kind. A *shape* is `{ n, cells: [[x, y], ...] }` inside an n×n box. A *piece* is `{ shape, x, y }`: a shape whose box has its top-left corner at grid cell (x, y). To draw a grid, loop over its cells and `rectfill` each non-zero one at `(x * size, y * size)`.

```js
s.board = grid.make(10, 20);
s.piece = { shape: grid.shape([".#.", "###", "..."]), x: 3, y: -1 };
// in update:
if (timers.repeatTick(s.leftRep, g.btn("left"))) grid.tryMove(s.board, s.piece, -1, 0);
if (g.btnp("a")) grid.tryRotate(s.board, s.piece, 1);
if (timers.tick(s.fall) && !grid.tryMove(s.board, s.piece, 0, 1)) {
  const over = grid.place(s.board, s.piece, s.color) > 0;
  const lines = grid.clearRows(s.board);
}
```

### `grid.KICKS`
The default list of `[dx, dy]` offsets `tryRotate` tries, in order, when a turned piece doesn't fit where it is: in place, one left, one right, one up, two left, two right. It's frozen. Pass your own list to `tryRotate` for different behaviour; `[[0, 0]]` means no kicks at all.

### `grid.make(w, h, fill?)`
Returns a new w×h grid with every cell set to `fill` (default 0, empty). Keep it in state. It's plain JSON, so `probe()` can return it, or a summary of it such as the filled-cell count or `fullRows`, for checks.

### `grid.inBounds(grid, x, y)`
Returns true if (x, y) is a whole-number cell on the grid. Use it before reading neighbours, or to keep a grid-walking player on the board.

### `grid.get(grid, x, y, outside?)`
Returns the value at cell (x, y), or `outside` (default -1) when the cell is off the grid. Because -1 isn't 0, "is this cell free?" checks (`get(...) === 0`) treat the edges as walls without a separate bounds test.

### `grid.set(grid, x, y, v)`
Sets cell (x, y) to `v`. Off-grid writes are ignored silently, so pre-filling levels or spawning blocks near the edge can't throw.

### `grid.shape(rows)`
Builds a shape from rows of characters, written like a sprite: `"."` or a space is empty, and any other character is a cell. The box size `n` is the larger of the number of rows and the longest row, and rotation turns the shape inside that box. Pad with `"."` to choose where it pivots: `["....", "####", "....", "...."]` makes a 4-long bar that turns around the middle of a 4×4 box. Make shapes once, in `init` or as constants.

### `grid.rotate(shape, turns?)`
Returns a new shape turned clockwise by 90° `turns` times (default 1; negative turns go counter-clockwise) inside its n×n box. Four turns give back the original, and `rotate(s, 1)` followed by `rotate(.., -1)` undoes itself. It doesn't check the board: use `tryRotate` to turn a piece in play, and `rotate` to build a shape's other orientations ahead of time or to draw a preview.

### `grid.cellsAt(shape, x, y)`
Returns the grid cells `[x, y]` the shape covers when its box sits at (x, y). Use it to draw a piece (`for (const [cx, cy] of grid.cellsAt(p.shape, p.x, p.y)) g.rectfill(...)`) and in `probe()` to show checks where a piece is.

### `grid.fits(grid, shape, x, y)`
Returns true if the shape, with its box at (x, y), lies entirely on empty cells and inside the left, right and bottom walls. Cells above the top row (y < 0) count as free, so a new piece can start partly above the board. This is the test behind `tryMove`, `tryRotate` and `dropDistance`. Call it yourself to check a spawn point, for example "game over if the new piece doesn't fit".

### `grid.tryMove(grid, piece, dx, dy)`
Moves the piece by (dx, dy) if it fits there, changing `piece.x` and `piece.y`, and returns true. Otherwise it leaves the piece alone and returns false. A false from `tryMove(board, p, 0, 1)` means the piece has landed. Pair it with `timers.repeat` for held left and right, and with a falling timer for gravity.

### `grid.tryRotate(grid, piece, turns?, kicks?)`
Turns the piece by `turns` quarter-turns clockwise (default 1; -1 is counter-clockwise). If the turned shape doesn't fit in place, it tries each `[dx, dy]` in `kicks` (default `KICKS`) and uses the first that fits. It changes `piece.shape` (and x, y if kicked) and returns true. If nothing fits, the piece is unchanged and it returns false, which is a good moment for a "bonk" sound.

### `grid.dropDistance(grid, piece)`
Returns how many rows the piece can fall before it lands (0 if it's already resting). `piece.y += grid.dropDistance(board, piece)` is an instant drop. Drawing the piece's cells at `piece.y + dropDistance` gives a landing preview.

### `grid.place(grid, piece, v)`
Writes the piece's cells into the grid with value `v`, so the piece becomes part of the board. Cells above the top row are dropped, and their count is returned. More than 0 means the stack has reached the top, which is the usual game-over test. Make the next piece after placing.

### `grid.fullRows(grid)`
Returns the row indices, top to bottom, that have no empty cell. Call it before `clearRows` when you want to flash or sparkle the rows first, or to score by how many rows cleared at once. Probe it in checks such as "a full row disappears".

### `grid.clearRows(grid, rows?)`
Removes the given rows (default: every full row), moves everything above them down, and adds empty rows at the top. Changes the grid in place and returns how many rows it removed. Duplicate or out-of-range indices are ignored. For a "pop" effect: `const rows = grid.fullRows(b)`, animate for a few frames with a timer, then `grid.clearRows(b, rows)`.

### `grid.stickStep(g, p?, held?)`
Reads player `p`'s stick (default 1) as one grid step, `[dx, dy]`, or null when there's no input. By default it uses `g.btnp`: one step per press, which suits menus and step-by-step movers. With `held` true it uses `g.btn` and steps every frame the stick is down, so slow it with a timer or use `timers.repeat`. Up beats down beats left beats right, so a diagonal gives a single axis. Use it for a grid-walking player, a menu cursor, or a piece-moving direction.

## timers: frame counts, repeats, blinking

```js
s.fall = timers.timer(timers.seconds(0.8), true);   // in init
if (timers.tick(s.fall)) grid.tryMove(...);           // in update
timers.restart(s.fall, Math.max(6, s.fall.len - 4));  // speed up
```

### `timers.seconds(s)`
Converts seconds to frames at 60 frames per second, rounded to a whole frame. Write durations in seconds when the spec does ("the speed goes up every 30 seconds"), so the code reads like the rule.

### `timers.timer(frames, loop?)`
Returns a timer `{ len, left, loop, done }` that fires after `frames` frames (at least 1). With `loop` true it fires every `frames` frames, forever, which suits gravity, spawners and blinking. Otherwise it fires once and sets `done`, which suits delays, invulnerability after a hit, and how long a pop animation lasts. Keep it in state and `tick` it once per update.

### `timers.tick(t)`
Advances the timer one frame and returns true on the frame it fires. A looping timer starts its next run; a one-shot timer sets `done` and returns false from then on. Call it exactly once per update for each running timer. Calling it twice makes time run double speed.

### `timers.restart(t, frames?)`
Starts the timer over, clearing `done`, optionally with a new length. Use it to rearm a one-shot timer, or to change speed: `restart(s.fall, s.fall.len - 2)` makes pieces fall faster from the next step.

### `timers.progress(t)`
Returns how far through its current run the timer is, from 0 (just started) to 1 (fired). Use it to drive animations from a timer: the size of a growing sparkle, a flash that fades, a countdown bar.

### `timers.every(g, n, offset?)`
Returns true once every `n` frames of the console clock (`g.frame % n === offset`). It's for cosmetic rhythms that don't need their own state, such as a sparkle every 8 frames. For blinking "PRESS START", `g.frame % 60 < 30` is simpler. Use a real `timer` for anything a rule depends on, since `g.frame` doesn't restart when a new game does.

### `timers.repeat(delay?, rate?)`
Returns an auto-repeat `{ delay, rate, held }` for a held button or direction. It fires on the press, then again after `delay` frames (default 12), then every `rate` frames (default 4). This is the familiar "tap to nudge, hold to slide" feel for moving a piece or a cursor. Keep one per button you need it on, per player.

### `timers.repeatTick(r, down)`
Feed it the repeat and whether its button is down this frame (`g.btn("left", p)`). It returns true on the frames the action should happen. Letting go resets it, so the next press fires at once. Call it once per update per repeat, even when the button is up.

## score: points, lives, saved high score

`g.save()` keeps one JSON value per cart. These helpers treat it as an object with named fields, so the high score can share the save with other things (settings, unlocked levels) without overwriting them.

```js
s.score = score.newScore(g, { lives: 3 });       // in init, and at each new game
score.addPoints(s.score, 100 * lines);
if (score.loseLife(s.score) === 0) { score.commit(g, s.score); flow.go(s.flow, "over"); }
```

### `score.loadField(g, key, fallback?)`
Returns the saved value under `key`, or `fallback` (default null) if nothing is saved, the save isn't an object, or the field is missing. Use it to read any saved setting, e.g. `loadField(g, "level", 1)`.

### `score.saveField(g, key, value)`
Saves `value` under `key` and keeps every other field already saved. If the existing save isn't an object, it's replaced with `{ [key]: value }`. Throws, like `g.save`, if the result isn't JSON or is over 4 KB. Saving writes storage, so call it on events (a game ends, a setting changes), never every frame.

### `score.newScore(g, opts?)`
Returns a fresh score `{ score: 0, lives, best, newBest: false, key }` for a new game. `lives` defaults to 3. `best` is the high score saved under field `key` (default `"best"`; use another key, such as `"best2"`, for a separate high score per mode). Call it in `init` and again whenever a new game starts, so `best` always reflects the save. For two players, keep one score each; with the same key they share one high score.

### `score.addPoints(sc, points)`
Adds points to the score (negative points take some away, but never below 0) and returns the new score. When the score passes `best`, it raises `best` and sets `newBest` to true, so the HUD can show the live high score and celebrate. It doesn't save; call `commit` when the game ends.

### `score.loseLife(sc, n?)`
Takes away one life, or `n`, never going below 0, and returns the lives left. 0 means game over: commit the score and go to the game-over screen.

### `score.gainLife(sc, n?, max?)`
Adds one life, or `n`, capped at `max` if given, and returns the lives now. Use it for a bonus life every so many points or for a pickup.

### `score.isOver(sc)`
Returns true when no lives are left. It's handy in `probe()` and in update guards.

### `score.commit(g, sc)`
Saves the score as the new high score if it beats the one already saved, keeping other saved fields, and returns true if it saved. Call it once when the game ends, not every frame. Saved high scores persist across restarts and power cycles, so checks can test "the high score survives a restart" with `t.reset({ keepSave: true })`.

## flow: title → play → game over

A flow is `{ mode, t, prev }`. `mode` is the current screen (any string you like: "title", "play", "over", "paused"), `t` counts frames since entering it, and `prev` is the screen before. In `update` and `draw`, switch on `s.flow.mode`.

```js
flow.tick(s.flow);
switch (s.flow.mode) {
  case "title": if (flow.startPressed(g, s.flow)) { newGame(g, s); flow.go(s.flow, "play"); } break;
  case "play":  playUpdate(g, s); break;
  case "over":  if (flow.startPressed(g, s.flow)) flow.go(s.flow, "title"); break;
}
```

### `flow.newFlow(mode?)`
Returns a flow starting on `mode` (default `"title"`). Keep it in state and expose `mode` from `probe()`, so checks can assert things like "pressing START on the title starts the game" or "losing the last life shows game over".

### `flow.go(flow, mode)`
Switches to `mode`, remembers the old one in `prev`, and resets `t` to 0. Going to the mode you're already in restarts its count. Reset the game state (new score, empty board) yourself when entering play.

### `flow.tick(flow)`
Counts one frame in the current mode and returns the count. Call it once at the top of `update`. Use `flow.t` for timed screens, such as returning to the title after 10 seconds of game over (`if (s.flow.t > timers.seconds(10)) flow.go(s.flow, "title")`) or a "READY?" pause before play starts.

### `flow.startPressed(g, flow, opts?)`
Returns which player pressed to start: 1, 2 and so on, or 0 for nobody. Presses in the first `after` frames of the mode (default 30, half a second) are ignored, so a kid still mashing buttons when the game ends doesn't skip the game-over screen. `buttons` defaults to START and A, and `players` to every controller the console has (`1..g.players`; on the cabinet that is just player 1). If two press on the same frame, the lower number wins. Returning the player lets "whoever presses starts" or "press to join" work with no extra code.

## turns: take turns, pass the controls, one score each

Games are single player unless the spec says otherwise. When it says two or more people play, they usually take turns, because the cabinet has **one controller** (`g.players` is 1; a desktop may have more). These helpers make that work on any number of controllers: when there are fewer controllers than players, everyone plays on controller 1 and a "pass the controls" screen goes up between turns; when each player has a controller, they use their own. A turns object `{ count, up, round, rounds, scores, passing, t, pass }` is plain data you keep in state: `up` is whose turn it is, `scores[p - 1]` is player p's score, `passing` is true while the pass screen is up.

```js
s.turns = turns.newTurns(2, { rounds: 3 });         // in init / new game
// update:
if (turns.waiting(g, s.turns)) return;              // pass screen up: nothing else moves
if (turns.btnp(g, s.turns, "a")) jump(s);           // the player who is up, on their controller
if (fellOff) {
  turns.addScore(s.turns, s.height);
  turns.next(g, s.turns);
  if (turns.isOver(s.turns)) flow.go(s.flow, "over");
}
// draw:
if (turns.drawPass(g, s.turns)) return;             // drew the pass screen instead of the game
g.text(`P${s.turns.up}  ${s.turns.scores[s.turns.up - 1]}`, 4, 4, g.colors.white);
// game over: const w = turns.winner(s.turns); // 0 is a tie
```

Read input through `turns.btn`/`turns.btnp` rather than `g.btn(b, 2)`, so the same cart works on the cabinet and on a desktop with two controllers. Expose `up`, `round`, `scores` and `passing` from `probe()` so checks can test "after player 1's turn it's player 2's" and "each player keeps their own score". Checks run on one controller by default; `t.reset({ players: 2 })` tries two.

### `turns.newTurns(count?, opts?)`
Returns turns for `count` players (default 2, at most 8), with player 1 up, round 1, every score 0 and no pass screen. `opts.rounds` is how many rounds make a game (each player gets that many turns), or 0 (the default) for no limit. `opts.pass` says when the pass screen shows: `"shared"` (default) only when players share controllers, `"always"` (a "PLAYER 2'S TURN" screen even with separate controllers), or `"never"` (you handle hand-overs yourself). Call it in `init` and again at each new game.

### `turns.shared(g, turns)`
Returns true when there are fewer controllers (`g.players`) than players, so everyone plays on controller 1. Use it to change the words on screen ("pass the controls" vs. "your turn") or skip a hand-over pause.

### `turns.controller(g, turns, p?)`
Returns the controller player `p` plays on (default: whoever is up): 1 when players share, otherwise `p`. Use it when you need `g.btn` directly, e.g. `grid.stickStep(g, turns.controller(g, s.turns))`.

### `turns.btn(g, turns, b)`
Returns true while button `b` is held by the player who is up, on their controller. It is always false while the pass screen is up, so a hand-over can't move anything.

### `turns.btnp(g, turns, b)`
Returns true on the frame button `b` is pressed by the player who is up. False while the pass screen is up.

### `turns.next(g, turns)`
Ends the current turn: the next player is up, and after the last player the round number goes up. It resets `t` and puts the pass screen up when the controls change hands (per `pass`). After the last round `isOver` is true and further calls change nothing. Returns who is up now. Reset that player's things (position, timer) yourself.

### `turns.waiting(g, turns, opts?)`
Runs the pass screen. Call it at the top of `update` and return early while it's true. It is true while the pass screen is up, and also on the frame the next player takes over by pressing A or START (`opts.buttons`) on their controller, so that press doesn't also jump or fire. Presses in the first `opts.after` frames (default 30) are ignored, so a button mashed as a turn ends doesn't skip the screen. Returns false (and does nothing) when no pass screen is up.

### `turns.drawPass(g, turns, opts?)`
If the pass screen is up, draws it over the whole screen and returns true; otherwise draws nothing and returns false. It shows "PLAYER 2" (or `opts.names[1]`, e.g. `["ALINA", "OWEN"]`), "YOUR TURN", "PASS THE CONTROLS" when players share, and a blinking "PRESS A" once presses count. `opts.color` (default yellow) and `opts.bg` (default night) set the colors. Call it at the top of `draw` and return when it's true; draw your own screen instead if the spec describes one.

### `turns.addScore(turns, points, p?)`
Adds points to player `p`'s score (default: whoever is up) and returns the new score. Points may be negative; a score never goes below 0. Throws for a player who isn't in the game. For lives or a saved high score per player, keep a `score.newScore` per player as well.

### `turns.isOver(turns)`
Returns true once every round has been played (only when `rounds` was set). Check it after `next` to go to the game-over screen.

### `turns.winner(turns)`
Returns the player with the highest score, or 0 if two or more share it. Show "PLAYER 2 WINS" or "IT'S A TIE" on the game-over screen.
# Recipes

Each recipe goes from a spec rule to the code, the probe and the check. The functions are in `runtime/lib/REFERENCE.md`; the named cart shows the whole thing.

## 1. Title → play → game over

> At 0 lives the game-over screen shows within 30 frames.

```js
flow.tick(s.flow);
if (s.flow.mode !== "play") {
  if (flow.startPressed(g, s.flow)) {
    if (s.flow.mode === "title") newGame(g, s);   // fresh score, positions, timers
    flow.go(s.flow, s.flow.mode === "title" ? "play" : "title");
  }
  return;
}
if (score.loseLife(s.sc) === 0) { score.commit(g, s.sc); flow.go(s.flow, "over"); }
```

Probe `mode`. Every check starts on the title, so begin with `start(t)`: `t.step(31)` (START is ignored for 30 frames), press START for 1 frame, `t.step(2)`. All three carts.

## 2. Thing A destroys thing B

> Touching a comet takes away one life and removes that comet. For the next 90 frames comets can't hurt the ship.

```js
timers.tick(s.safe);                                   // one-shot timer(90), done = not safe
const hits = collide.resolve([s.ship, ...s.things], [{ a: "comet", b: "ship", kill: s.safe.done ? "a" : "none" }]);
if (hits.length && s.safe.done) { g.sfx("hit"); timers.restart(s.safe); score.loseLife(s.sc); }
s.things = collide.alive(s.things);
```

One rule entry per "who destroys whom" sentence; blink in `draw` while safe. Probe `lives` and `safe`; check by steering into a comet (recipe 6). `carts/dodge`.

## 3. Spawn things and get harder

> Comets start at 1 pixel per frame and get 0.5 faster every 600 frames of play, up to 3.

Write the curve as one function, `speedAt(played) = min(3, 1 + 0.5 * floor(played / 600))`, and count play frames in state (`g.frame` doesn't restart with a new game). Spawn on a looping timer at `x: g.W`; drop things once off screen. Check real movement: probe, `t.step(1)`, probe. `carts/dodge`.

## 4. Bounce a ball

> The ball bounces off the top, bottom and right walls and never goes past them.

```js
b.x += b.vx; b.y += b.vy;
if (b.y < TOP) { b.y = TOP; b.vy = -b.vy; }
if (b.y > g.H - B) { b.y = g.H - B; b.vy = -b.vy; }
if (b.vx < 0 && collide.overlap(b, pad)) { b.x = pad.x + pad.w; b.vx = -b.vx; }
```

Clamp when you flip, or the ball sticks in the wall; bounce off the paddle only when moving toward it. Check frame by frame that the ball stays inside and `vy` flips at each wall. `carts/paddle`.

## 5. Grid movement and pieces

> Tapping a direction moves the gardener one tile; holding it repeats after 12 frames, then every 6.

Size the board from the screen, `grid.make(Math.floor(g.W / T), Math.floor((g.H - TOP) / T))`, then move when `timers.repeatTick(s.rep, step !== null)` fires for `step = grid.stickStep(g, 1, true)` and the target is `grid.inBounds`. Pieces on a board use `shape`, `tryMove`, `tryRotate`, `place` and `clearRows` (REFERENCE.md). Probe positions and counts, not the whole board. `carts/collect`.

## 6. Checks that play the game

> Stepping onto a gem adds 10 to the score.

A check is a tiny bot: read the probe, pick the input, step a few frames, repeat until it happens or a frame limit runs out.

```js
async function chase(t, max, done) {
  for (let n = 0; n < max; n += 2) {
    const p = await t.probe();
    if (done(p)) return p;
    const c = p.comets[0];
    await t.input([{ frames: 2, p1: c ? (c.y > p.ship.y ? "down" : "up") : "" }]);
    await t.step(2);
  }
  return t.probe();
}
```

Error messages say what was expected and what happened. Saved best: end a game, `await t.reset({ keepSave: true })`, probe `best`. Sounds: `(await t.sounds()).length`. Screen size: `p.W`, `p.H`.

# Writing checkable rules

A cart's `spec.md` is the source of truth (start from [template.md](template.md)). Its **Rules** are what the kid asked for, written so someone can check each one. There are two kinds:

- `(auto)`: the playtest proves it by pressing buttons, stepping frames and reading the game's state. Every auto rule needs a check in `checks.js` ([checks-format.md](checks-format.md)).
- `(you check)`: a person judges it on first play, answering yes or no on the cabinet. Use this for looks, feelings and fun.

Write rules before code, and change the spec first when the game changes.

## The form

```md
- R1 (auto): Holding right moves the frog 2 pixels per frame; it stops at the right edge.
- R2 (you check): The frog looks happy when it catches a fly.
```

- One rule per list item. Longer rules continue on lines indented by two spaces.
- Ids never change and are never reused. To drop a rule, delete its line and say why in the Changelog; its number stays unused. New rules take the next number after the highest one ever used (a fork continues from its parent's).
- Nothing but rules goes in the Rules section. Notes go in Assumptions.

## What makes an auto rule checkable

A good auto rule names **what happens**, **when** (in frames; the game runs at 60 per second), and **what you can see in the game's state** afterwards. If you can't picture the check, it isn't an auto rule yet.

| Bad | Why | Good |
|---|---|---|
| The controls feel responsive. | A feeling. | (auto) Pressing left moves the paddle 3 pixels left on the next frame. |
| You can catch the fruit. | When? What then? | (auto) When the basket touches a fruit, the fruit disappears that frame and the score goes up by 10. |
| It gets harder over time. | How much, when? | (auto) The rocks fall 1 pixel per frame faster every 600 frames, up to 6 pixels per frame. |
